extracted.intended_audience: orators, poets, and writers; students of rhetoric and literary style
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing 'the Sublime' in rhetorical and poetic composition: how choice of thought, figures, diction, and structural devices create grandeur and emotional force. Aimed at those composing speeches, poems, histories, and narrative passages seeking elevated style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of sublimity: abrupt (Demosthenes) vs diffusive (Cicero)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sublimity of Demosthenes is generally sudden and abrupt: that of Cicero is equally diffused."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt, vehement, rapid, and terrible style (like Demosthenes) when you wish to exaggerate or rouse vehement emotion and carry the audience with you. Use a diffusive, widespread, long-burning style (like Cicero) when you wish to overpower by a flood of language—suitable for familiar topics, perorations, digressions, description, history, and natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of great writers as a path to sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: The emulous imitation of the great poets and prose-writers of the past can carry an author into sublime heights; this is not plagiarism but drawing inspiration from master-works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix rivalry on high examples (Homer, Plato, Demosthenes, Thucydides) to guide and elevate your composition. Imagine how great predecessors or future ages would judge your work to spur effort and achieve 'ripe perfection.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of images (imagery) to work on the emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Images (in the broader sense) are thoughts presented so that speaker imagines seeing what he speaks of and produces a similar illusion in hearers; poetical images are designed to astound, oratorical images to give perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ images to add energy and passion; in poetry allow mythical exaggeration, but in oratory prefer energy and reality. Avoid poetical impossibilities in argumentative oratory because they may seem monstrous or offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratorical images must be energetic and real
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief beauties of an oratorical image are its energy and reality; mingled with practical argument they not only convince but enthral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, vivid, believable images embedded in argument (e.g., Demosthenes' prison/escape image) to paralysing judgment with passion and carry the audience beyond mere logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of speech lend force but require judicious use
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures, judiciously employed, play an important part in producing sublimity; but their use may arouse suspicion of artifice and dishonesty if misapplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy figures where they appear natural and are supported by sublimity and passion to avoid alienating judges or readers. Excessive or ill-placed figures create distrust or seem like sophistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe / adjuration (addressing absent or divine figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure of adjuration or apostrophe exalts subjects (e.g., invoking ancestors) and by a bold appeal can lift a speech to the loftiest altitude of grandeur and passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ adjuration in moments of supreme exaltation to inspire heroic pride and to momentarily supersede argument. Must be used in the right place, manner, occasion, and motive — otherwise it is merely an oath and lacks grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful use of oaths and careful word choice in them
rubrics_metrics.description: An oath's grandeur depends on being employed in the right manner and choosing words that avoid giving opponents a handle (e.g., Demosthenes carefully omits 'conquered').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When swearing or invoking, select phrasing that cannot be easily rebutted; adapt the oath to reinforce rather than weaken your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and interrogation (rhetorical Q&A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternating question and answer reproduces meeting objections and the moment of passion; the orator replies to himself as though meeting another's objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical questioning and self-answer to raise tone, make speech convincing, and give an appearance of spontaneous feeling. It blinds judgment by simulating passionate extemporaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of connecting particles (asyndeton) for rapidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The removal of connecting particles gives a quick rush and 'torrent rapture' to a passage, making the writer seem left behind by his own words (asyndeton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use asyndeton to imitate agitation, distress, or swift motion; examples include rapid lists of verbs without conjunctions. Effective for urgency but must fit occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of figures to multiply energy
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of different figures, when two or three unite, mutually contribute to the vigour, cogency, and beauty of a speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine repetition, broken clauses, asyndeton, hyperbaton, etc., to vary movement and avoid stillness; e.g., Demosthenes' broken repetitions imitate blows. Vary to preserve force and keep audience engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over‑regularizing with conjunctions (which curb passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binding the language with conjunctions (Isocrates' logical sequencing) smooths away abruptness and destroys the impression of mechanical impulse that passion requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor irregularity and broken clauses in passionate passages; too much logical linking reduces rapidity and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbaton (transposition) to imitate agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition of words or thoughts from their usual order (hyperbaton) bears the stamp of violent mental agitation and imitates real emotional speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transpositions and suspensions to create suspense, the sense of unpremeditated danger, or urgency; authors like Thucydides and Demosthenes employ it boldly. Overuse risks incoherence, but when timed well it is astounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition, enumeration, contrast, and climax
rubrics_metrics.description: The juxtaposition of different cases, the enumeration of particulars, and the use of contrast and climax add vigour, diversity, movement, and elevation to style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ lists, contrasts and climactic ordering to increase momentum and emotional effect; vary case, tense, person, number, and gender for rhetorical dynamism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plural for singular to magnify effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Plurals used for singulars sometimes create an impression of vast number and more impressive dignity (e.g., using plurals to express multiplied calamity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this device when the theme permits amplification or exaggeration; it rouses imagination by suggesting multiplicity where only one is meant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract many particulars into one singular for dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraction of plurals into singulars can create an appearance of great dignity by knitting scattered particulars into a corporate whole (e.g., 'all Peloponnesus was divided').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use singularization to give weight and corporate life to a set of particulars; appropriate when you want unity and solemnity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historic present to dramatize narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: When past events are introduced as happening in present time, the narrative becomes dramatic action (historic present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the historic present to make readers feel as spectators within the scene; it imparts immediacy and dramatic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange of persons / direct address to involve reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Interchange of persons (second-person address, direct appeals) places the reader in the midst of the perils described and makes them a partaker in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address individuals directly or shift persons to rouse interest and fix attention; this personal thrust makes readers feel implicated and present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden shift to the first person or speaking-in-character
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden step from third-person narrative into the first or into a character's speech strikes like an outburst of passion and is effective in urgent crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit tags such as 'he said' when attributing a sudden threat or outburst; this leaves the writer 'behind his words' and intensifies immediacy. Use for urgent or highly charged moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis (circumlocution) adds dignity but risks feebleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis often sounds in concord with a literal expression and lends dignity and melody to thought, but it is very liable to abuse and can seem inflated and vapid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periphrasis to harmonize and elevate simple expressions (e.g., 'destined journey' for death) but restrain it—excessive circumlocution leads to feebleness and disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures may provoke distrust; disguise with sublimity and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures have a tendency to rouse suspicion of artifice; to allay this distrust we must call in the powerful aid of sublimity and passion so that art passes beyond suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that rhetorical devices are supported and overshadowed by genuine grandeur and passion so that their artificiality is hidden—like light putting lesser lights out of sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of appropriate and striking words (diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of appropriate and striking words has marvellous power; beautiful words are the very light of thought and endow facts with a vocal soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select diction that matches subject matter and emotional intent; avoid imposing language on trifling subjects (a grand style on small matter is grotesque).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poetical/fabulous mould in argumentative oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical and fabulous language that runs into impossibilities becomes offensive and monstrous in oratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain reality and practical persuasiveness in oratorical images; reserve mythic exaggeration for poetic contexts, not for argumentative addresses to judges or critical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and broken clauses to imitate action and agitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition and broken-up sentences (repeating words and breaking sentences) imitate agitation and motion (e.g., 'by gesture, by look, by tone...'), preserving the force of repetition by continual variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured repetition with variations and broken syntax to simulate physical or emotional blows and to keep rhetorical energy. Avoid mechanical repetition without variation, which weakens effect.
